subtopic: MR. AIKEN  RESPONSIBILITY FOR EMPLOYMENT POLICY IN PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS
MR. AIKEN  RESPONSIBILITY FOR EMPLOYMENT POLICY IN PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which affects all hon. members of the house. Yesterday, as reported at page 6066 of Hansard, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, the Minister of Public Works advised the house that he had given instructions that in future all elevator operators in the centre block of the parliament buildings should be bilingual.
My question of privilege is that it does not lie within the authority of the minister to set employment policy within the precincts of parliament. The minister's duty is to provide staff, not policy. Policy is and must be the sole responsibility of parliament and its officers.
I am not commenting on the decision that was made. I am merely challenging the right of the Minister of Public Works to rise and advise the house what the employment policy of parliament will be. It is the principle to which I take strong objection.
If the minister alleges that he has this authority, then I intend to take action to change it, and I so give notice now. If some of my friends from Quebec would say that I am against bilingualism on parliament hill, let them think twice. If this particular minister can on his own whim give such an order, a future minister could not only reverse it but could give entirely new direction in employment practices.
I say this is not the personal prerogative of any minister, and I rise to protest his taking this authority to himself. It is repugnant to parliament that it should not control policies within its own walls.

In the purchase of defence equipment and supplies, is a preference given to suppliers who provide Canadian content and, if so (a) upon what authority is such preference based (b) what is the extent of such preference for Canadian content compared with non-Canadian content?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Under provisions of the Defence Production Act, the Minister of Defence Production is responsible for ensuring that the necessary production capacity and materials are available to support the Canadian defence production program. Accordingly, departmental officers always look to Canadian companies for the provision of supplies that are required for our defence program and examine requirements to determine how these needs may contribute to the creation of Canadian skills and facilities. It is a provision of the general conditions that are applicable to departmental contracts that to the full extent to which they are procurable, consistent with proper economy and the expenditious carrying out of the contract, Canadian labour, parts and materials shall be used in the work. Therefore, the department buys from Canadian firms if practicable and only turns to other sources of supply when procurement from the Canadian sources is deemed to be uneconomical or impractical. For example, the complexity of certain weapons systems is 20220-387
Questions
such that production in Canada for our limited requirements often involves prohibitive costs. In these cases, the department encourages Canadian firms to participate in production sharing arrangements with the United States and defence export arrangements with NATO and other friendly countries.
In addition, it is the government's policy that in the absence of strategic reasons, a premium will be paid for a product with higher Canadian content. This premium is calculated at 10 per cent of the difference in foreign content. In the case of coal, a premium of up to 20 per cent can be paid.

I have received quite a few telegrams from turkey organizations. Perhaps at this time I should make a short explanation of the position of the government.
On July 17, 1957 import restrictions were placed on the movement of turkeys into Canada. This action was taken for a number of reasons, but essentially because a flood of United States turkeys was threatening the existence of the Canadian turkey industry. It was at that time that the eviscerated, oven ready turkey was just coming on the market. The United States producers were a little ahead of our producers in this technical advance, and they began sending this new poultry product into Canada in such numbers and at such low prices as to seriously threaten the Canadian industry.

speechtext: I think that the Minister of Agriculture should be replaced.

['Extensive forestry resources are to be found in the provinces of New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Nova Scotia and, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, in both New Brunswick and Nova Scotia these resources are easily accessible, and therefore have much greater potential from the development point of view.
At the same time, one of the important aspects associated with forestry is the conservation measures that must be adopted if we are to be able to have the assurance that depletion and wholesale exploitation will not be the end result, with a most necessary and desirable industry disappearing from our area. Better forestry management practices must come and these can only be brought about through educating the population in the provinces in good forestry practices, and through legislation which places restrictions on the manner in which the products from the forests are utilized.
I was interested to note the comments in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald yesterday, July 28, by Nova Scotia's minister of lands and forests, Hon. E. D. Haliburton, who is reported as saying: "The Nova Scotia government is concerned about the quality of forest management on the province's crown lands." He had a good deal more to say, but I have no time to place it all on record. However, I have no doubt it would be of interest to members of this committee and I would refer them to the article in question.
We have the good fortune on Cape Breton island to have seen established in recent years the Nova Scotia Pulp Company which has been utilizing the products of our forests in Nova Scotia, especially from the island of Cape Breton. At the same time we have seen an increasing emphasis on the exporting of lumber to markets overseas. This has resulted in added employment for the people of my area. We have also seen the development of a forestry program by the government of Nova Scotia, in co-operation with the Department of Forestry in Ottawa, initiated during the period when the Conservative party held office, to have the double-barrelled effect of utilizing our forests to the greatest possible', 'degree and providing employment to displaced miners thrown out of work by the actions of the Dominion Coal Company. This program has proven to be highly successful, to the degree that this government has adopted the program established by the former Conservative administration. However, substantial delays in reaching agreement with the province of Nova Scotia have been evident since this government assumed office. I would like to hear an explanation from the Minister of Forestry as to why these delays have occurred, in view of statements by Premier Stanfield of Nova Scotia that his government is ready and willing to proceed at any time on the basis of the agreement originally reached by the former administration and his government. Certainly hardships were created because of the dilatory attitude of this government in arriving at an agreement with the government of Nova Scotia.
The people of my area and the people of Cape Breton generally are now facing further serious problems as the result of the intended action of a coal operator to curtail coal mining operations on Cape Breton island. The end result can only be more unemployment, hardship and poverty unless immediate action is taken by this government to initiate programs which will provide employment for those thrown out of work. Certainly one of the programs that would assist in this regard would be increased emphasis on the forestry program already in effect. In this regard, I might say that officials of the united mine workers of America will be meeting with Premier Stanfield tomorrow, and among the matters to be discussed is the forest stand improvement program for displaced or unemployed miners. Associated with this forest stand improvement, in my opinion steps should be taken by the present minister to establish a forestry research station on Cape

Breton island. This research station would be designed to increase forest research work throughout the Atlantic provinces. Not only would this station involve itself with the conservation of all of our forest resources but it would also endeavour to increase production and develop new products. It would also endeavour to carry out an educational program in our public schools which would make our young people more aware of the potential of this primary product and provide them with a better appreciation for the utilization of it. It should also endeavour to exert influence on the private owners, both large and small, of our forest lands so that they might better appreciate the importance of conservation and the revitalization of our forest lands.
In conclusion, may I extend to the Minister of Forestry a very cordial invitation to visit Cape Breton island as soon as he can, and see for himself what has been accomplished through the forest stand program. As a result of what he sees he will possibly be more encouraged to establish the forest research station which I have suggested. I thank the rest of the committee for the kindness they have shown in listening to me and, of course, I thank the hon. member for Kootenay East.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Yesterday, when I dealt with the consequences of the steps taken by this government with respect to Mr. Banks, I have been quoted as saying, as recorded in the fourth paragraph, right hand column, at page 6083 of Hansard for July 28, 1964:
-decisions were taken.
Now, as I was then referring to courts, it is obvious that I said:
-decisions were rendered.
Mr. Chairman, there is a most important point on which I want to call the attention of the house. As recorded in the sixth paragraph, right hand column, at page 6084 of Hansard, I am quoted as having said the following words:
In my opinion-I was talking about the $25,000 bail-this is sufficient guarantee-
Mr. Chairman, quoting the hon. chief justice who rendered the decision and fixed the bail, I said:
It was, in the opinion of the magistrate, a sufficient guarantee to make sure that Mr. Banks would be present at the time of the hearing of his appeal.
Consequently, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the remarks I just made should be taken into account in order to make the necessary corrections at pages 6083 and 6084 of the English version of Hansard for July 28, 1964, in respect to the adequate amount of the bail, because I have too much respect for the courts to discuss the terms of the judgment.
In fact, Mr. Chairman, I had just said that the chief justice of the Quebec appeal court, Hon. Lucien Tremblay, was in my opinion one of the most experienced jurists. I respect his decision and it is not up to me to discuss its consequences.
All I said was that, in his opinion, the setting of the bail at $25,000 was enough.

In ordinary circumstances I would be delighted to make some observations in connection with many of the departments which I presume will be under survey as we consider interim supply at this time. However, it is not my intention to do this. I intend to confine my remarks to the Department of Forestry. I regret the absence of the minister-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Where is he?

-but
that is something over which I have no control. I am glad to take the word of the acting minister that he intends to pinch hit for his colleague, and this gives me a great deal of pleasure.
I preface these remarks with a bit of personal observation in connection with the Department of Forestry, because it was my great privilege to be the first minister of that department. During those years I acquired a great respect for the personnel of the department; I acquired a great respect for all the dedicated public servants who serve our country through the medium of the Department of Forestry. It was a matter of great satisfaction to me that before I retired as the minister of that department I was able to secure the services of the present deputy minister of forestry, Dr. Rousseau. He came to Ottawa to serve his fellow citizens in another capacity after having served for quite a long time as a very prominent member of the faculty of Laval University. It was a great pleasure to me that he decided to make this change. I am sure there will be no difference of opinion in this house in regard to the fact that the public service in general is very fortunate to have the services of Dr. Rousseau in this capacity.
Hear, hear.

I realize that when people examine departments and members are looking at departments they are inclined to measure the efficiency and importance of a department by the amount of money the department spends. In my opinion that is altogether a wrong measuring stick to use. In my opinion a department should be judged by the service it renders to the general economy of the country, and in my view the Department of Forestry is rendering fine service in this connection.

Interim Supply
Canada is a forest nation. I would like to remind the house of the importance of the forest industry and place some figures on the record in connection with it, because I do not think we are reminded often enough of the contribution which is made by the forest industry in general to the economic health of this nation. I find that the total forest area is about 50 per cent of the total area of all Canada; it is something like
1.700.000	square miles. I find that the productive area included in those 1,700,000 square miles is about 1 million square miles. I acknowledge immediately that 80 per cent of that area is administered by the provinces; but I believe the federal Department of Forestry is working very closely in co-operation with the provinces in connection with their administrative problems, with the general result of an improvement in conditions so far as the health of the industry is concerned.
We have 170 species of trees native to Canada. Thirty one of these are softwood, mostly evergreens. May I remind the committee that we have an annual crop-this is not a diminishing asset-of 3,200,000 cubic feet of timber year after year that may be continued if it is properly looked after. So far as employment is concerned, the forest industry takes care of about 300,000 people; it provides steady employment for this number. It pays out per year $1.2 billion in salaries and wages. As a part of this, the woods operations take care of something like
80.000	people, and that particular phase of the forest industry pays out $350 million in cash. So I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that I have no hesitation in putting these figures on the record because I think we need to be reminded of the importance of this great industry.
We have small and medium size saw mills all over the country, and we have a few large one. It may be a surprise to hon. members within the sound of my voice today to learn that there is a total of something like 8,000 saw mills; that the saw mills employ something like 50,000 people; that the total payroll of the saw mills alone is about $150 million; that the value of the saw mill products is something like $750 million, or three quarters of a billion dollars. These figures refer to saw mills alone.
Then we come to the pulp and paper industry, which one might say is sort of the aristocrat of the forest industry. I do not concede that myself, because I was practically brought up in a saw mill; nevertheless it is generally recognized that the pulp and 
paper industry, because it processes to the ultimate the products of our forests, does earn a tremendous amount of dollars for this country. May I remind you, Mr. Chairman, that the pulp and paper industry is Canada's leading manufacturing industry. We have some 130 pulp and paper mills, and the sale value of the products is about $11 billion per year, or $1,500 million. The pulp and paper mills of Canada employ 65,000 people; their wages and salaries amount to $350 million.
That is not all, Mr. Chairman; I am just getting nicely started. We have the ancillary industries, that is the industries using wood as their principal raw material, manufacturing finished and semi-finished products with an annual sale value of $800 million. These ancillary industries employ 70,000 people in full time jobs. The industries to which I refer are furniture factories, planing mills, veneer and plywood plants, and so on.
Again I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that I am not finished. We also have the paper using industries. The sale value of the products of these paper using industries is $500 million. The items manufactured include paper boxes, paper bags, building paper, coated papers, stationery supplies and sanitary papers. As I have said, there is a sale value of products of half a billion dollars under this heading, and these industries employ 29,000 people.
I have not told the whole story even with all the figures I have just put on the record. I say to the committee that the products of the forest which are manufactured in Canada are of great importance, but may I also say that the contribution made by that industry by way of the exportation of its products is certainly on a comparable level. Today the value of the exports of the forest products industry is $11 billion, $1,500 million, or about 30 per cent of Canada's total exports. We import less than $300 million, and the purchase of the things which we have to bring into this country is made possible by the exportation of forest products.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I go to the question of the exportation of lumber before I finish this particular phase of my remarks. We export a matter of 4,200 million feet of lumber a year, to a value of something like $300 million. This lumber is shipped to about 50 different countries.
The point I am trying to make is simply this; that we as Canadians need to be reminded of the importance of our forest industry, the part it plays in the general economy

of Canada and the part it plays in bringing about our ability to import things which we have to buy. In other words the industry makes a tremendous contribution to our balance of payments position at the present time, which is in a position it will probably always be in because we have to borrow money outside the country. Then of course, having borrowed it we have to pay interest on it, so obviously we have to export to live. Therefore from the point of view of employment the industry is tremendusly important. From the point of view of annual production and the furnishing of material for the ancillary industries it is equally important, and as I say its contribution to our balance of payments position in this country is great.
I acknowledge right away that in order that we shall maintain that industry and that it shall grow and flourish as it should, and in order that we as Canadians can contribute to its growth, we must have trained people. In this country there are four universities offering professional training in this regard, and I would list them in order of importance from my own point of view, although I realize there might be some disagreement about this. The four universities in Canada which offer professional training in forestry are, first of all, the University of New Brunswick, second the University of British Columbia, third Laval University and last the University of Toronto. In addition we have the maritime forest ranger school in Fredericton; the Ontario forest ranger school at Dorset, Ontario; the forest ranger school, department of lands and forests, at Edmonton, Alberta; the lakehead college of arts, science and technology, in Port Arthur, Ontario; station fores-tiere de Duchesnay, Duchesnay, Quebec; the conservation officer training school at Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; and the forest ranger school at New Westminster, British Columbia. These are the schools and universities which represent the media of education which makes a contribution to the continuation of this most important industry.
As I have stressed the importance of this industry, I think at this stage we might ask ourselves this question. What do we intend to do to preserve this industry which is so vital to Canada? In this regard we have some deadly enemies of the industry, but perhaps the No. 1 enemy is the forest fire menace. The average forest fire loss in Canada for the period 1951-60-and I stress that this is the average, Mr. Chairman-was 293 million cubic feet. But in 1961 alone, which was a very bad year from the standpoint of
Interim Supply
forest fires, 2,650 million cubic feet of lumber was consumed. The total utilization of lumber in that same year-in other words, production-was 3,277 million feet. Therefore it will be seen that we allowed, if that is a fair statement, almost as much timber to burn in the year 1961 as we cut for all the pulp and paper mills and saw mills in the country.
I am not being critical of the department and the things they are doing. Neither am I critical of the provincial departments. I think they are reasonably efficient, probably as efficient as they can be in the circumstances. That did happen to be a bad year, I know. However, I think from year to year we are learning to combat this menace more efficiently than we have over the previous few years. In other words I am quite satisfied that we are improving-and I now speak in a national sense-in combating this deadly menace called forest fire.
In my remarks so far I have stressed the importance of our forests in an economic sense, but there are also other functions which the forest performs for the people of Canada. For example, it performs the function of a regulator of water resources. As you know, Mr. Chairman, as a result of snow lying on the ground in the winter, moisture is given off in the spring of the year. If this moisture, which is allowed to flow as nature demands, is protected or contained by forest cover and trees it will run off much more slowly than if the land were "hard cut", as we say in the lumber business.
I suggest to the acting minister that this is a matter of importance. I realize he has had a lot of experience and does not need any advice from me, but I know he will not mind receiving a little advice. I submit that he might convey to the department my own feeling that one of the most important functions which they have is the use of their influence to bring about a proper cutting program. When I say proper cutting, I mean a cutting which will lend itself to a retention of the water resources of the country over a period of months, rather than letting it run off quickly.
Next, our forest is the habitat of wild animals and birds as well as a place of recreation, sport, boating, fishing, etc. In my opinion there is need for the regulations to be framed with the assistance of the department, and' this also applies to the spraying of our forests.
I should like to say a word about consideration for animals and birds in our forests during the spring spraying program. The present mixture which is being used for budworm,

Interim Supply
spraying in New Brunswick would appear to be exceedingly harmful to birds. In this connection I respectfully suggest that there be careful examination of spraying material with a view to eliminating ingredients which are harmful to all life of this type. I examined the history of the damage which was done in New Brunswick by spraying fish, and the federal government of that day took legal action against the government of the province of New Brunswick to secure damages for the harm done to the fish in the province.
This is all ancient history now, and over with, but apparently those in authority decided they would try to make the ingredients a little less harmful to the fish, and an improvement was brought about. But may I say to my hon. friend the acting minister that apparently the improvement which was made so far as the fish were concerned has been brought about by adding a very dangerous, damaging and destructive ingredient to the spray mixture as far as birds are concerned.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
That does not apply to fish, does it?

No, I am
talking about birds. I acknowledge and am grateful for the change that was made and I take some little credit for having a part in the change that was made with regard to the strength of the mixture inasmuch as it certainly relieved the situation so far as fish are concerned. But now I am asking him to look after the birds and I am sure that with that kindness of heart for which he is famous he will do all he can.
I come now to what is being done for the industry by the department. I have talked about the importance of the industry to Canada and now I should like to say something about what Canada is doing for the industry. First of all, I notice in the estimates that the department is contributing $600,000 to the laboratory at Pointe Claire. In my opinion this is the right type of research because it is a combination of research by private enterprise and assistance by the government. It is my opinion, for whatever people may think it is worth, that this combination of the two provide the right type of research. Research in this regard should either be exclusive to the government or else exclusive to private industry, with assistance by way of grants from the government. I congratulate the govern-

ment in this regard. The policy, of course, is one established by the former minister and government so perhaps we can also take some of the credit.
This year we are again continuing grants to the provinces amounting to almost $8 million. These grants are for various purposes, one of which is the making of an inventory and production of inventory figures. An overall provincial inventory is maintained and the federal government pays a proportionate share of the cost. It also reimburses the provinces to the extent of $15 per 1,000 trees planted, $4 per acre seeded with ground preparation and $2 per acre seeded without ground preparation. In 1962-63 there were 36 million trees planted on 56,000 acres. I presume that in the future this will undoubtedly be a part of the ARDA program. If that is not the case the programs are very similar in any event and the same minister is responsible. I suggest that he consider reforestation as a part of the ARDA program. Without a doubt, improvements in forestry go hand in hand and in many instances the soil is more suitable for the growing of trees than for any other crop.
I have made reference to forest fire protection and I do not want to weary the committee by elaborating any more on that subject. I want to take a minute to refer to the general concept of roadbuilding and the building of airstrips because in my opinion this is something that will bring about the possibility of bringing in raw material from greater distances. It will make it possible for private enterprise to do this, whereas they would not be able to do so if they had to bear all the expense of constructing a means of access to these isolated areas. I do not want to elaborate further except to say that in every place where stand improvement has been undertaken in Canada it has been a tremendous success.
With regard to forest research an amount of $2,642,000 is to be appropriated to cover technical staff and expenses. I think we have to acknowledge the fact that without a doubt we are in competition with the world in forest products and in order to maintain our competitive position we must of necessity have the very latest in research and in technical advice. So I am very pleased to see this amount being appropriated by the government at this time.
With respect to forest entomology and pathology, over $5 million is to be spent this year and, so far as the destruction of our forests is concerned, these services are al-

most equally as important as the prevention of forest fires. I happen to know that if steps had not been taken in the province of New Brunswick in 1951 to do something about the budworm menace we would have had terrific destruction of our forests and undoubtedly many forest areas would have been almost completely destroyed by this pest. So these operations are continuing with the very capable staff that is available for this work and which we are fortunate to have at our disposal in Canada.
Forest products research is concerned with new products and I am sure that the amount to be appropriated will meet with he approval of all hon. members. I realize that my time is almost up but I should like to repeat that this year the forestry department will spend :$19i million, part of the money in outright grants and part in payment for services rendered, which services are available to private industry.
May I refer for a moment to what I consider is a very fine piece of research that is under way at the present time. I refer to mechanical research. I regret and deplore the fact that people are being put out of work because of automation, but the fact remains that in order to be competitive we must recognize that we have to use the same methods to accomplish the same thing as are being used in other places. Recently it was my privilege to talk to one of the gentlemen in the forest products laboratory in Ottawa. I thought he had a tremendous fund of mechanical knowledge, which is available of course to the people of Canada, especially those who are interested in this industry.
I am sure the money that will be paid in outright grants and the money spent for services which are available are most proper expenditures because they mean that Canada is in partnership with everyone who is in business today. The government collects approximately 50 per cent of any profits and I think it is very appropriate that they should render some service in consideration of the fact that they are in partnership to that [DOT]extent.
Mr. Chairman-
Carried.
Dispense.
-some people seem "to be in terrible rush to vote $700 million.
We want a holiday.

I am not interested in holidays.

May I ask the hon. member a question? Do I understand from his remarks that he considers this is the opportunity and the occasion on which to examine the spending of the government?

Speaking to the point of order, may I say that in the supplementary estimates there is an item dealing with forestry. The main estimate for forestry has not been considered by this house. The administration of that department can be discussed by the committee of supply. The minister who is responsible for it should give an accounting of what he is doing and his plans for the future. The fact that a vote was passed in the main estimates dealing with ARDA does not affect the question of the administration of the department. We have not concluded the discussion on the Department of Forestry. Surely on that basis a person can deal with a subject which is under the jurisdiction of the minister.
If the President of the Privy Council is listened to, we would be prohibited from debate on so many occasions just because we had passed a certain item. Are we not now to ask questions of the Minister of Agriculture because the estimates of his department have been passed? The thing is ridiculous. A question was asked today and he gave a lengthy answer to it.

Mr. Chairman, I note that on page 6089 of Hansard, the last item relates to an additional one twelfth for agriculture, item 60, and according to the main estimates item 60 relates to irrigation, water storage projects and prairie farm rehabilitation. Actually this is the same as ARDA. I think the hon. member who has the floor now is entitled to deal with the matter.

Mr. Chairman, this vote has been dealt with. If I remember correctly, we

discussed the estimates of agriculture for seven or eight days. The Minister of Forestry was here-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Five days; why don't you be accurate?
Well, it might have been five days.
He is an auctioneer; he is entitled to expand a little bit.
My hon. friend must have been putting in his crop or bringing in the hay because we did not see hide nor hair of him. I am sure he is completely out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Hum-boldt-Melfort-Tisdale referred back to vote 60 which was passed in total on July 10, 1964. It is not before the committee at this time, and neither is vote 65.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder if I may ask this question. Is the Minister of Foresty in charge of ARDA? If that answer is yes, then a discussion of the administration of the ARDA program is appropriate during a discussion of general supply.

That part of his administration was dealt with. He was here and he made a quite lengthy statement. He answered the
questions that were asked and the vote was passed.

It is all very well for members to try to suppress the freedom of speech. I should like to read to you, Mr. Chairman, from Hansard for July 28 when this house was asked to go into interim supply. The committee was asked to vote a sum amounting to $696,010,791.01. There was a long list of departments including health, water, natural resources, and so on. Certainly, my remarks, merely because they contained a reference to ARDA, should not raise such great fear on the government benches. If I am allowed to proceed with my speech, I see no real objection being voiced by the government benches. Never before have I known my words to strike such fear into so many government cabinet ministers who have risen to try to suppress my few remarks regarding the administration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member, on reflection, will agree there is something to the point raised by the minister. It is, however, a borderline case because we have an unusual situation where an item coming under a department whose estimates have not been passed was considered as part of another department, whose estimates have
Interim Supply
now all been passed. I am referring of course to the Department of Agriculture. I fully realize that the estimates of the Department of Forestry have not been before us and have not been passed. On that account I can agree with the hon. member that we can discuss that department's administration, but we are still bound by standing order 59(2) which says we have to be strictly relevant to what is before us. Items 60 and 65, dealing with ARDA, have already been disposed of and therefore cannot be before the committee of supply at this time.
However I would think members of the committee would want to be generous to the hon. member who has the floor and allow him to make passing references to the subject inasmuch as they relate to the administration of the forestry department, which can be properly discussed at this time. If the hon. member wants to take that into account we will get along well.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to proceed. If I get carried away I am sure you will bring me back to order. If you do not, then I am fearful cabinet ministers and government members will rise in their places in the hope of cracking down on anything that might be pointed out that is detrimental in regard to their administration.

Would the hon. member permit a question dealing with something he said earlier before the point of order was raised? With reference to the $700 million we are being asked to vote now, he said he was more interested in examining these expenditures than in having a holiday. How does he reconcile that view with the statement made by the house leader of the official opposition, as recorded at page 5985 of Hansard for July 24 when, discussing future business of the house, he said:
Would the government like to consider three months, if we complete the dominion-provincial fiscal measure and pass interim supply in short order, and then adjourn?
From that statement it would seem to me members of the official opposition would be much more interested in a holiday than the hon. member says now.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say anything about a holiday.
I should like to answer the question.

He did
not ask any question.

Interim Supply

He asked how I reconcile my views with granting three months supply. I am in complete agreement with granting three months interim supply because it would facilitate and speed up operations in the house. The people of the country are completely fed up with the way parliament has been going on in the last couple of weeks. We will do everything in our power to aid the house leader in bringing in legislation.
Oh, oh.

We suggested time and time again bring in this legislation and we will pass it, bring in that legislation and we will pass it; and we did on every occasion. They laugh over there. That is why I say bring in three months interim supply and we will pass it.
And then we will adjourn?

Well, that is your decision, not mine. I intend to speak on the administration of the Department of Forestry. I was interested to see the Minister of Agriculture in his seat today because even though ARDA now comes under the Department of Forestry, it used to be under his jurisdiction. But because his own department was late in putting out his biography, the Prime Minister did not realize he was such a great man and took the whole department away from him for 17 or 21 days, or something like that.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Mr. Chairman, I would sooner hear speech No. 7 than the one we are getting because we have heard it so many times.

That is auctioneer
talk.
You know all about it.

I don't follow that speech No. 7 bit. Maybe he wants me to bid eight; I don't know. It is very interesting to see the minister back and taking an interest in ARDA. It is too bad he did not take a bigger interest in it, as he would still have it in his own department. If he had only written that biography sooner he could have convinced the Prime Minister and the other cabinet ministers just what a great "I am" he is.
The Alberta government has taken a rather shameful and niggardly attitude with

regard to ARDA. In 1961 and 1962 they said it was nothing but a hoax, and many people in Alberta feared that ARDA would be doing nothing more than enlarging P.F.R.A. and perhaps slowing up development under P.F.R.A. An article in the Financial Post of August 17, 1963, was headed: "Our Not-So-Good Earth May Yet Yield Surprises. All 10 provinces and Ottawa are involved in a mammoth comeback project. If it works Canada's entire economy should benefit."
Dealing with Alberta it said:
Alberta has been slow to take up ARDA projects but favours additional development of dams and irrigation systems.
It pointed out that one of the wealthiest provinces in Canada is more interested in better land irrigation and water conservation than in ARDA projects, and I think that is a rather shameful approach on the part of such a wealthy province.
Out of 464 applications for ARDA projects only 24 have come from Alberta, and I point out that some of the provinces, Nova Scotia in particular, are asking for a better share in the cost sharing arrangements with regard to the projects. I quote from the Chronicle-Herald of Halifax, May 9, 1964:
They feel that the formula by which the provinces and Ottawa share the costs of the program on a 50-50 basis is unfair and unrealistic, that different conditions and different levels of income in each province require differing degrees of federal aid.
Alberta, one of the wealthiest provinces in Canada, is second lowest in the number of ARDA projects applied for by all provinces, and I point out that the lower half of my constituency is an area in which ARDA could play a tremendous part. Rehabilitation began in that area in the 1930's. The whole area was settled in 1909 and 1911, but people moved out of it from 1920 to 1935, and in 1935 the federal government participated in a gigantic movement of the people from that area. Many of the residents still there now look to ARDA for hope in the future.
There has been far too much talk with regard to getting the farmers off the land and creating farms of an economic size. As a result of an approach of this kind, they hope to see fewer farms and fewer farmers. This is definitely the wrong approach. One of the aims of this legislation was to put marginal land to more profitable use. Another was to improve the income and opportunities of many of those who live in rural areas. A third object, and perhaps it is the most important one, was to conserve water and soil in Canada. Certainly, a province as

wealthy as Alberta should be in a good position to spend money in order to develop and conserve its water and soil resources, but when I look at the southern half of my constituency I become somewhat frustrated by the attitude taken by the Alberta government with regard to the development of this area. If we go about the administration of the ARDA program in a proper way, so as to create greater employment opportunities in many rural areas and provide for the proper use of land, this will certainly encourage more farmers to enter agriculture, because when land is used to better advantage it is obvious that more farmers will be able to find a living from it.
As I travel across Canada I meet many people who have moved off the land. There should be one hope and one dream. It is that as a result of the correct administration of ARDA they will be able to find their way back to the land. I say this because there is no better life than one which derives from the land, whether as a farmer, or as a rancher or as one engaged in any similar type of occupation. Certainly, I should like to see more people brought back to the land in circumstances which would make it possible for them to enjoy a standard of living comparable with that of people engaged in any other type of occupation. But this can only be accomplished if the act is administered with this objective in mind. Many people in Alberta think that the act is now being administered in such a way that certain projects which could have been proceeded with under P.F.R.A. are being held up and labelled as projects which might be proceeded with under ARDA. This being so, before any concrete action can be taken there must be lengthy discussion between individuals in the locality which would benefit as a result of the project, and officials of the provincial government. Then in turn the matter must be taken up with the federal government. The delay caused by these discussions tends to hold up almost indefinitely a project which might well have been proceeded with under P.F.R.A. almost immediately, the federal government paying nearly all the cost. The arrangements I have described may be all very well in connection with a large program which P.F.R.A. cannot by its very nature handle. But I believe many of these smaller projects should proceed under P.F.R.A. as they have done in the past.
Many clauses now included in the ARDA agreement have a tendency to limit the size
Interim Supply
of projects recommended, and these should be changed.
I notice, Mr. Chairman, that the interest which was shown at the beginning of my speech has fizzled out. I see now only about eight Liberals in the chamber. It is amazing to note how they tried to suppress me and then fled.
Ten.

I guess two more have popped in.
It is true of course that the agreements are only effective until 1965, at which time they must be redrawn. When we consider the lines upon which the act should be administered and the effect of these agreements upon its administration, we must ask ourselves whether the agreements should be confirmed or whether a better deal should be given to the provinces. The Montreal Gazette of July 6, 1964 suggests that the federal government intends to hold talks with the provinces in August and early September on this subject. The administration of the act will be discussed, together with various projects which, it is felt, might well come within the provisions of the measure but which at the present time do not. According to the Regina Leader-Post of May 29, 1964, the Minister of Forestry has said that the provinces may get more than they do at present. What proposal has the hon. gentleman in mind? Does he intend to propose something along the lines of the suggestion by the Nova Scotia minister of agriculture, that more should be made available to the provinces which are less fortunate than others, or will grants continue to be made on the standard fifty-fifty basis? I know it is really not laid down as such, but in practice it works out to that.
I mentioned certain provisions which limited the operations contemplated under the act, particularly with regard to the approval of projects. I should like to draw attention to section 4, for instance, which provides that except with the approval of the governor in council no allotments to a province for soil or water conservation projects shall exceed 50 per cent of the allotment of the province, and that at least 10 per cent of the total allotment shall be allocated to research projects, rural development studies, and so on. I think this provision as to 50 per cent is unnecessary and I believe that to some extent it limits the scope of ARDA and restricts its administration. I believe many provinces should look upon ARDA from a much wider

Interim Supply
point of view than they do at the present time. I have read many of the pamphlets which the Department of Forestry has put out on the subject of ARDA. Most of them tell us that ARDA projects should spring from the grass roots-that they should have a local beginning, and that local committees should be set up to visualize the best way in which communities could be developed, such committees to report their recommendations to the provincial governments. This is all right, but perhaps the scope envisaged in these arrangements is not large enough. It is possible that provincial governments do not encourage local communities to set their sights high enough. Maybe the local people do not appreciate the possibilities and scope of the ARDA program; perhaps they do not know what amount of money the provincial government is prepared to expend as its share of an ARDA program.
Let us consider water conservation, for example. A local community may suggest damming a small creek. But in the years to come such a dam may prove too small; it may be made useless by a larger and higher dam built to serve a wider community. This is why I think the section I have mentioned, together with certain others, should be examined closely to make sure they do not limit the size and scope of many projects which it is desirable that ARDA should undertake. The present is a good time at which to do this. Hon. members need hardly be reminded of the drought which exists, particularly in Saskatchewan and southern Alberta following the hot, dry month of July. Many farmers and ranchers are having to sell their livestock or haul water to them. Now is the time when all the authorities concerned should become very active and interested in bringing aid to these localities. As one of the pamphlets put out by the department says, the local people must be behind these schemes in order for them to be successful. Certainly the local people are in desperate need of water conservation measures, and this is the time for provincial governments to move so as to satisfy these needs.
Certainly the provincial government must be consulted; but I think the federal government, in the administration of ARDA, should provide leadership and encouragement to the provinces. I know they are providing quite a bit of encouragement, but still the province of Alberta lags far behind all other provinces in Canada in respect of having ARDA projects approved by the federal government. I know that in fact every program for which they applied up until March 31

was approved by the federal government; but they have been reluctant to spend money on the development of the basic resources of that province, namely land and water.
Certainly the province of Alberta has been very fortunate in its resources under the ground. The oil companies have found a need for many of the resources below the ground and this has brought an unlimited supply of wealth to the province, but the province has been reluctant to return that wealth to the people through the development of its resources of land and water.
The Minister of Agriculture has now left the chamber, but I would hope that on the trip he proposes for the agriculture committee-which I think is to come about in October and with regard to which I have already said in this house that I am opposed and think it is a waste of money-the committee will take a good look at the land east of Calgary to the Saskatchewan border. I hope they will take a good look at the great productive value that lies in the future for this whole area, a great productive value that is now not even being tapped. If the committee does this, they will certainly get some idea of the great potential of this area. I know there are many other areas throughout Canada that this agriculture committee will no doubt visit, if the trip ever comes about. I would hope they would visit some other areas which have a potential, such as the area east of Calgary to the Saskatchewan border, and perhaps even on into Saskatchewan.
The minister has been making suggestions with regard to a revision of the ARDA program. As reported in the Regina Leader-Post of March 19, the Minister of Forestry said that the way in which each farm assistance program under the act must be authorized by federal authorities will probably be revised. In other words, the federal government is going to give a blank cheque to the provincial governments which they can spend in any way they see fit. This might be all right, but certainly along with it should go the rider that the provincial governments must spend the money on aims set out by the ARDA legislation.
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry if I have offended the ruling you gave at the beginning of my speech. While I well realized that the agriculture estimates had been passed, and with them the ARDA estimates, I felt that due to the severe drought conditions existing in southern Alberta and northern Saskatchewan, and the administration of ARDA and what it can mean to these areas, I should

raise this point in the house at this time in order that we can have less talking and more action under this very worth-while piece of legislation.

Mr. Chairman, without any desire to prolong unnecessarily this debate on interim supply, in view of the fact that the debate on this motion will likely cause our study of the main estimates to be held up until after the parliamentary recess-to which we all look forward-I wish to take advantage of this opportunity to deal with an important subject that I had intended to raise on the estimates of the Department of Justice.
The battle to protect Canadians' rights has been long and constant, but fortunately occasionally successful. Government activities have expanded to the point where members of legislatures have been unable to do all the work personally, in some cases, that they should do in this field. They have delegated many of their duties to appointed boards and commissions-it is the nature of the development of our society that has caused this-and have too often failed to provide any appeal to the courts from the decisions of such bodies. The result of these circumstances has frequently been injustice. Fighting the arbitrary decision of a board is so costly as to be beyond the purse of the average citizen. A few of my own constituents have written me to this effect just recently. One who fought, however, was a Mr. Frank Roncarelli of Quebec. He had been deprived of his licence by the Quebec liquor commission on orders from Premier Maurice Duplessis because he had provided bail for arrested Jehovah's Witnesses. He could not sue the commission because the act establishing it prevented such action, so he sued the premier. It took 11 years and most of his wealth, but he won a decision from the Supreme Court of Canada that was a milestone on the Canadian road to freedom. That eternal vigilance which is the price of liberty has been constantly necessary. As one who believes in the maintenance of freedom and the rights of citizens, I wish to direct the attention of the committee to the gradual erosion of our freedom in this country as the result of legislative and administrative action.
I wish to mention first of all a bill recently passed by the legislature of British Columbia, which is known as an act to establish the British Columbia hydro and power authority. I will go into detail later, but I just want to say that in my opinion, when a provincial legislature becomes involved in a prointerim Supply
gram that withdraws from the electors who created it some of their basic rights and freedoms, it is our responsibility to protest, and suggest a remedy. We have had numerous illustrations throughout our history of the transgression of the rights of the subject in this country. Time will not permit me to deal with those at any length; but I do wish to remind the committee of the vigorous fight the late J. S. Woodsworth made against section 98 of the Criminal Code. It was because of J. S. Woodsworth's leadership in that fight, supported by the members of this party throughout the years, that the Criminal Code was amended.
Only recently we have had protests from members on the opposition side of the house, including some of my colleagues, with respect to injustices caused by the administration of the Immigration Act. Then quite recently as far as legislative action is concerned, I am sure most of us remember the infamous bill 99 that was presented to the Ontario legislature at the last session by the now departed attorney general. I mean departed from the legislature; I do not wish him any further departure. This bill was withdrawn at the insistence of vigilant people and vigilant members of the legislature who took exception to it. In this case I give full credit not only to the members of my own party but to the members of the Liberal party who saw this threat to personal freedom in this country. I also give credit to the members of the Ontario press in this particular instance.
Bill 99, the police state bill, shocked Ontario citizens into compelling their government to withdraw it, because it proposed the most blatant invasion of private rights which had occurred in that province. It was not the first such attempt. It should come as a considerable relief to those who value their civil rights and liberties that the attorney general of the province, Arthur A. Wishart, has since that time publicly recognized this fact.
I want to deal with another illustration of an invasion of the rights of the citizen. It is not an invasion which will cause any hardship or suffering to any citizen of the province of Alberta, but it is an invasion of their rights and of their privacy. I should like to quote from the Ottawa Journal for June 8, 1964 to which I hope my hon. friend from Alberta will listen, because I know he is a vigorous defender of the rights of the citizen, and I am sure my reference to this act passed by the legislature of Alberta will cause him to have some qualms. This is what

Interim Supply
an editorial which originally appeared in the Lethbridge Herald has to say:
Daylight saving time a crime.
The Alberta government, in its almighty arrogance, asked (and obtained) approval of the legislature not only to make daylight saving time illegal in Alberta, but to make it an offence, punishable by a $25 fine, for any person to "use or observe" the time on any watch or clock that is fast or slow.
Most people would like everything advanced by perhaps an hour in the summertime, so they could enjoy more of the lovely Alberta mornings and have more leisure in the evening daylight.
The Alberta chamber of commerce is asking the provincial government for a province-wide plebiscite on the issue at the time of the next municipal election.
That is the very least the government can agree to.
But if it refuses to make that concession, isn't there some municipality somewhere that will hold a plebiscite anyway and defy this autocratic government?
Imagine. A $25 fine for "using or observing within the province any time other than mountain standard time". Crowns have fallen for less than that.
I mention this to illustrate that this is an unnecessary interference with the private lives of our citizens. I can well imagine that there is many a farmer in Alberta who wishes to get up early to milk his cows and puts his clock on fast time. Whom is he harming in doing this? But apparently, under the present legislation in Alberta, if he does this he will be subject to a $25 fine. It is a very small thing, but it is this creeping form of the invasion of our citizens' rights by actions of the legislatures of this country, and by administrative acts, which should be giving us increasing concern.
Now I want to deal with the latest illustration of the legislative expression of the autocratic frame of mind. I want to refer to a bill passed by the B.C. legislature on March 10, which is an act to establish the British Columbia hydro and power authority. This is blatant transgression of the rights of the citizen, of the farmers in this province, of the working people of the province and all trade union rights, which should be protested in the most vigorous manner in this house and wherever possible. I speak with conviction on this subject because I am one of those persons who would rather live on a modest scale than in luxury and surrender one iota of the freedom which has been achieved through the centuries.
I have discussed this bill with colleagues of mine in my own group. Our members have protested this legislation in the B.C. legislature. I have also discussed it with members of the official opposition and some
[Mr. Herridge.)
of the legal fraternity on the government side of the house. Listen to this clause which I am going to read, Mr. Chairman. This is section 1 of clause 53, dealing with the application of other statutes. It says:
Notwithstanding any specific provision -in any act to the contrary, except as otherwise provided by or under this act, the authority is not bound by any statute or statutory provision of the province.
Mr. Chairman, did you ever before hear of a clause like that contained in any measure in Canada? I have consulted parliamentary counsel and some lawyers in private practice, and they tell me that they do not know of any similar piece of legislation anywhere in Canada. This means that the B.C. hydro and power authority is placed above the legislature of British Columbia, with the exception of measures such as the arbitration act, the workmen's compensation act, the labour act and one or two others? With those exceptions under this clause the B.C. hydro and power authority is exempted from all statutes of the province of British Columbia. It is under this section of the act that the B.C. hydro and power authority is perpetrating injustice on hundreds of the constituents whom I have the honour to represent.
I have had numerous letters from my constituents residing at points extending over a distance of 150 miles expressing their fears and protests at the policy of the B.C. hydro and power authority with respect to relocation or compensation. Under this act the authority are going to offer these people who are being disturbed-flooded out as a result of the building of the high Arrow dam- market value for their property. I want to contrast this with the policy followed by the St. Lawrence seaway authority where people, their homes and community buildings were relocated under suitable circumstances to the satisfaction of the vast majority of them. The B.C. hydro and power authority refuses to relocate owners; they have offered these people, as I say, market value. What is market value in an area which is going to be flooded out?
I have previously mentioned the policy of the national capital commission, which has been very different from that proposed by the B.C. hydro and power authority. The national capital commission has considered all aspects of this question, and as with the Saskatchewan dam authority, people have been compensated on the basis of the potential value created by the development under consideration. In some cases I am informed-I

am waiting for all the documents in this respect-that around the Buffalo pond dam in Saskatchewan some of the farmers were paid $1,000 an acre for waterfront land, because they were waterfront properties which had great potential value owing to their recreational values in beaches, and other like attractions.
I mention this to indicate how people who think in these terms can gradually erode the freedoms and rights of the private citizen almost without his knowledge. There was very little said about this in the press at the time this act was passed in the B.C. legislature, and it is only now that the first victims of this intolerance, this overriding legislation, are beginning to realize what it means to them, and what it will mean to all of us if this type of thinking and policy is allowed to continue in the future.
Typical Bennett democracy.

Yes, that is so.
Now I want to deal with another section which to date has concerned the farmers in my constituency.
There is another section which is concerning labour organizations in British Columbia. I want to quote section 56. Do not forget that whenever we allow the rights of any individual to be taken away from him we are paving the way to having our own rights destroyed in the future. Section 56 deals with labour relations and reads as follows:
1.	Where a conciliation board has been appointed under the labour relations act to deal with a dispute between the authority and one or more of its employees or a trade union, the report of the conciliation board is binding in every respect upon the parties.
2.	No person shall declare or authorize a strike and no employee of the authority shall strike and the authority shall not lock out any employee or employees.
3.	Words and expressions used in this section have the same meaning as those words and expressions used in the labour relations act.
The labour unions concerned are fully aware of the meaning of those words. Subsection 4 reads as follows:
4.	Where there is a dispute between the authority and one or more of its employees or a trade union, section 29 of the labour relations act does not apply.
That is the section that protects the rights of the trade unionists in our province. What has been the reaction? I mention this at the request of numerous trade unions that are involved with this legislation. Here is a telegram that was sent to the chairman and members of the external affairs committee:
Interim Supply
The joint councils of the unions of hydro and power authority representing the 5,000 employees of this crown company unanimously request your committee declare ultra vires that section of bill 14 that denies hydro authority employees the right to strike as this is contrary to the principle of natural justice. Previous to the takeover of the British Columbia Electric Company by the provincial government said employees had all the rights that workers in the province enjoy, including the right to strike. We fervently urge the return of this right.
It is signed by John L. Hayward, chairman of the joint council of unions of the British Columbia hydro and power authority. Why has that section been placed in the bill? Whether it is a private corporation or a public corporation, the policy of the corporation is affected by the philosophy of the government in power, and that is why this legislation has been adopted. The B.C. federation of labour has taken up the matter and has protested vigorously against this most unfair and unusual legislation. While Premier Duplessis passed similar legislation in 1954 in the province of Quebec-
It was a shame.

I am very glad we are in agreement for once-and while we have this legislation being adopted in 1964 in British Columbia, we find that Quebec is doing away with such legislation. I have a quotation from the Montreal Gazette of Saturday, July 11 last. The headline is "New Law Would Allow Public Service Strike", and the article reads as follows:
Premier Jean Lesage served notice yesterday that the government intends to extend the right to strike to most of the public services in the province. He made the decision known in tabling a new series of proposed amendments to the government's controversial labour code, which is due to come up for final study in the legislative assembly next week.
The changes grant the right of affiliation and the right to strike to employees in most of Quebec's key public services, subject to a series of restrictions closely modelled on those contained in the Taft-Hartley act in the United States.
If the amendments are passed by the house as expected, employees of municipal and school corporations, hospitals, orphanages, universities, colleges, convents, telephone and telegraph companies, railways, transportation companies, gas, water and electricity services, garbage removal companies, etc., will all be given the right to walk off their jobs if normal negotiation procedures fail.
Why was this done? Premier Lesage, and I give him full credit for it, responded to the representations of the syndicates or trade unions of Quebec, and I give the officers of those unions full credit for standing up for the rights of their members. As I said before, I give full credit to Premier Lesage for

Interim Supply
responding so favourably to their requests. In Quebec in 1964 they are wiping out the Duplessis legislation of 1944.
I am sorry, it is 1954.
I have looked it up and the basic legislation was enacted in 1954.
I doubt that.

In 1964 in British Columbia they passed legislation similar to that supported by Premier Duplessis in 1954 and which is laying the foundation for the corporate state in B.C. I wish to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that sometimes when we are faced with the actions of a government and its agencies some people are inclined to say: What can we do about it? We can all do something about it if we accept some personal responsibility. I wish to give one illustration where vigilance brought results. I have here a quotation from the New York Times of Sunday, May 24, 1964. I always purchase the Times on Sunday afternoon to find out if the government has given away any more of Canada to the United States during the week. The article is an Associated Press dispatch from London. It is headed "Woman Wins Court Battle to Keep View of Thames", and reads as follows:
After a two year court battle by Miss Nancy Maurice, 63 years old, the London county council will eliminate eight stories from a block of apartments it plans to build across from her home. Miss Maurice can go on enjoying her view of the Thames river from the Battersea borough bridge.
Miss Maurice took one look at the specifications for the housing block when they came out in 1962 and went to court. She asserted the block, which she dubbed "the monster", would cut off the sunlight from her home, lower the value of her property and ruin the river view.
The high court of appeals held recently that she had just cause for complaint. The council is redrawing the plans. The building will be 157 feet tall instead of 220.
I mention this in order to illustrate what one person can do who sticks up for her rights. Our statutes and our common law are based on the common law of Great Britain and we can all do something in this parliament, in the legislatures, in the trade unions and in the farmers' organizations and women's organizations to make certain that these rights are not eroded and taken away by legislative or administrative action.
Therefore I urge members of parliament to be concerned about this question. It may not affect some of us directly at the present time but it is our duty to be concerned. I urge the legislatures to be concerned about this matter and particularly the people of British Colum-

bia, the farmers' organizations and the trade unions. I trust that they will continue to protest this infamous law so vigorously that at the next session of the legislature the premier of British Columbia will shamefacedly take action to have it withdrawn.
Mr. Chairman, as I have said before, I have nothing against these people as individuals, but collectively I have thought on occasion that they are a menace to society. That is just my personal opinion. I urge that the Minister of Justice study this piece of legislation carefully. There are many precedents for the disallowance of legislation passed by the provincial legislatures, and I urge the Minister of Justice to disallow this legislation.
No, you cannot do that.

I urge him to do so because it transgresses the principles of democracy and the Canadian Bill of Rights. I see my hon. friend does not agree. He is afraid that at some future time the Quebec legislature will pass a bill and there will be a danger of the federal government disallowing it. I say this, regardless of whether we live in Newfoundland or British Columbia, if the rights of any citizens of this country are transgressed by provincial legislation, government should have the courage to disallow it.
This brings me to my last point. I am not quite sure how much time I have left. I get a bit carried away with this subject. In my opinion, because of the increasing number of incidents of legislative autocracy and administrative dictatorship, there is a greater need for an ombudsman. He would deal with specific cases of misuse of authority by legislators and by agencies of government, by boards and commissions and, on occasion by individual civil servants who lose contact with the ordinary citizen.
You know, there is a tendency on the part of those who are particularly brilliant to lose some of their humanity in the process of exercising their intellectual ability. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, there is a great need for action on this score. I am not the only one to suggest this. The members of this group have previously recommended the need for an ombudsman in this country. Recently a former justice, Mr. Justice J. T. Thorson, spoke from experience following a panel discussion of this matter. I wish to quote briefly from the Ottawa Journal for May 14, in which I read:
Hon. J. T. Thorson, retired president of the Exchequer Court of Canada, Wednesday threw his

support behind a campaign to introduce the ombudsman system in Canada.
This former justice is supporting New Democratic party policy. I am glad to see that. This is the hon. gentleman who supported our nuclear policy. It is amazing how our influence is growing in this country.
The outspoken Canadian jurist took his stand in an interview at the annual meeting of the Canadian citizenship council following a panel discussion on how the system works in other countries and the need for it in Canada.
Mr. Thorson, president-elect of the council for 1964-65, said he supports fully the introduction in Canada of ombudsmen-officers of parliament or the legislatures who investigate complaints by individuals against unfair administrative decisions and, when necessary, recommend remedial action.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we have to take action to fight against this tendency towards legislative and administrative tyranny.
Before concluding I just wish to deal with a quotation from the Gazette for Friday, July 10, concerning Crichel Down. This deals with an incident in Dorsetshire in 1937, when a farmer was dispossessed of his land improperly by the British air ministry. There was a protest because it split his farm. Finally, as a result of the protests by farm organizations and support from the public, this situation was remedied. This editorial reads in part:
The British labour party says that if it is elected in October it will appoint an "ombudsman" a defender of the rights of the people against the misuse of authority by government officials. The Scandinavian countries established this office of "ombudsman". And other countries are coming to recognize its necessity.
Then in conclusion the editorial says:
But this is not simply a matter that concerns a Labour party and those who may live under its rule. This is a matter of concern to all those in all countries who feel the spread of officialdom over their lives. It is a very real problem in Canada. Canada needs its "ombudsman" too.
As Prof. W. H. Angus, of the law faculty of the University of Alberta, told the Canadian Bar Association at its annual conference last September: "If the present trend continues and administrative government tribunals are permitted to pursue whatever tickles their fancy, our society would seem destined to suffer some rather serious consequences".
The case of Crichel Down is the perfect example of what those consequences may be.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I once again urge the Minister of Justice to examine this infamous piece of legislation. I am sure if he does what we consider to be right he will disallow it. I urge this house to give consideration to the introduction of legislation that will provide for an ombudsman to protect the rights of Canadian citizens, to protect their

rights against the increasingly dictatorial powers of some government boards and commissions.

I want to take a few minutes to speak in this debate this afternoon because there have been a few remarks made by the hon. member for Acadia which some people who read Hansard may take as factual, unless the rest of the story is told. He was discussing, it seemed to me, during the main part of his remarks, the question of ARDA. He directed some criticism against the government of Alberta, stating they were dragging their feet with regard to getting approval from the federal government for projects under ARDA.
It is amazing to me to see this particular member, and other members of the Progressive Conservative party from the province of Alberta, taking such delight in constantly downgrading their own province. The facts respecting ARDA are that this act was passed by a Progressive Conservative government. It is a fact also that several months, in fact considerably more than a year after this act was passed, there were no regulations, no rules and no guidance at all for provincial governments or local authorities as to how they could proceed to present a project to the federal government for approval.
I inquired about this in September of
1962.	The act had been passed several months at that time. I asked how many projects had been submitted by the province of Alberta to the federal ARDA branch, and how many of those had been approved. There was no answer given by the federal Department of Agriculture which had responsibility for the act at that time. However, I did find out from the ARDA committee in Alberta that they had submitted about eight projects to the federal government at that time. They were awaiting some action by the federal government. As late as December of that same year, three months later, in spite of the fact that these projects had been prepared by some kind of local committee, but more particularly by the provincial ARDA committee, there was still no approval given by the minister of agriculture of that day.
In addition to that, Mr. Chairman, the federal director of ARDA for the Dominion of Canada, Mr. Davidson, was in Alberta.
In fact it was in Medicine Hat many, many months after the act was passed in this house, and during the course of his remarks and during the questions that were asked of him by people interested in what could be done under the act, his replies were constant. I

He said there was scope to do anything at all that would be helpful or useful to rural people any place in Canada, and there was authority granted by the federal government to undertake such projects.
This was months after the act was passed, yet he could offer no information as to how the local committees might be set up, no information or guidance as to what they should ask for, no information as to how much local support was necessary for a project, or how much provincial support would be necessary, nor could he say how far the federal government was prepared to go with respect to anything.
The hon. member for Acadia criticized the provincial government for not submitting some kind of project under ARDA for water and soil conservation in southeastern Alberta, because of the severe drought conditions at the present time. The federal government of that day was made up from the party my hon. friend supports, but even in spite of those severe conditions absolutely no action was taken by the government of the day to do anything about initiating ARDA projects to achieve what he calls water and soil conservation measures.
Which government implemented ARDA?
I cannot hear what the hon. member is saying. Would he speak out loud enough.

The hon. member suggests we did nothing while we were in government in 1961. Which government implemented ARDA? ARDA came into being in 1961, and the Suffield community project was initiated in that same drought year.

That is exactly the point I am making. The government of that day did in fact pass ARDA, but surely if it had intended any practical action to come from this it should have been willing to try to set up some kind of regulations and give some guidance for expediting projects. As I said, it was months and months after the act was passed, but the government of the day had not given any guidance as to how it was going to be implemented. In fact it gave absolutely no guidance as to what the federal government would accept.

Has the hon. member looked at the three year record from 1961, when the act was passed, until almost March 31, 1964? Of the 464 projects that were submitted by the ten provinces only 24 of them came from Alberta even though, according to the 1961 statistics, 20 per cent of the farmers in Alberta have an income of less than $1,200 a year.

Not one project submitted by the Alberta government has been turned down by the federal government as yet.

I don't understand this attitude of the federal members from Alberta, continually getting up and downgrading their own province.

On a point of privilege, the hon. member has said I have downgraded the province of Alberta. In no terms and in no words have I downgraded Alberta. It is the best province in Canada, but I think the government of Alberta has lagged a great deal in regard to the ARDA program.

Obviously, Mr. Chairman, there is no question of privilege, and the only point of order is the fact that the hon. member is continually interrupting when I have the floor and that, of course, is a violation of the rules.
