Exactly.
I would like to remind him that with regard to the development of irrigation and land and water use, no province on the prairies has spent as much money as the province of Alberta.
Much of it started before Social Credit came into power.

That might be so, but it has been carried on at an accelerated rate since Social Credit came into office. I want to put these few remarks on the record so that anyone reading Hansard would not take the statments of the hon. member as the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.
They are the facts. I can document them. There is no question about the whole truth.

The record of performance of the Progressive Conservative government in the administration and expediting of projects under ARDA has been something less than expected, particularly when one thinks in terms of the tremendous political propaganda carried on all over western Canada with respect to this act. We know for example that there were pamphlets printed at public expense prior to the passage of the act. I have said before and I will say it again that at that stage there was no justi-

speechtext: I shall have to ask the hon. member for Acadia to permit the hon. member for Medicine Hat to continue his remarks without being interrupted.

There are many things which the province of Alberta is doing in the administration of its affairs which happen to have tremendous public support. One would think that those members of parliament who come from the province of Alberta would give some support to that province, in the best interest of its citizens. But we do not seem to see any of this support coming forward.
One of the subjects I wish to deal with this afternoon, because it has been a sore spot with the government of Alberta and residents of that province for years, is the attitude of the Department of National Health and Welfare in applying the regulations governing the sharing of costs under the hospitalization program. I think it would be well for us to review briefly how this federal-provincial cost sharing program works, so that we may completely understand this discriminatory action on the part of the federal government both under the present administration and under the previous one. I might say this attitude is costing the residents of Alberta close to $2 million a year and, as I have indicated, it is unfair and discriminatory.
Under this co-insurance fee system, patients using the hospitals in Alberta in the year 1962-63 paid to the hospitals something over $5,700,000 in direct payments. Under the federal cost sharing program for hospitalization the federal government treats this revenue represented by the co-insurance fees as revenue payable directly to the hospitals, and therefore it is deducted before the balance of the cost becomes shareable by the federal government jointly with the province. We think this is unfair because it discriminates against those provinces which impose a patient fee or co-insurance fee instead of collecting hospital revenue by means of sales tax or a hospital insurance premium, or some other form of direct taxation. In our view, there is a definite advantage to the co-insurance fee system as compared with the prov-

Interim Supply
ince collecting some direct tax to meet hospital costs.
Today in Alberta the individuals using our hospitals are paying only 7.8 per cent of the operating costs. The municipalities-and I wish to give the complete picture; this is a four mill tax, plus any extra requisitions they have to meet-pay 11.9 per cent of the operating costs; the province pays 40.6 per cent of the costs, and the federal government 39.7 per cent. As far as we are concerned it is no business of this parliament to dictate to the provinces how they shall collect the portion which is paid by the provinces and to disallow these deterrent fees, or co-insurance fees, and subtract them from the actual operating costs of hospitals before the balance of cost is shared. In my opinion, this represents a direct attempt at interference with the way in which the province of Alberta chooses to run its affairs. I hesitate to become involved in the politics of the situation, but it just happens that in the province of Alberta the government, in its administration of the affairs of the province, has greater support from the residents than any government in Canada. Yet the department of health and welfare-

Would the hon. member permit a question? Will he tell us, while he is talking about provincial government finances and the position taken by the federal government, what has brought about the resignation of the Alberta government's treasurer?

The hon. member for Acadia, in his determined effort to downgrade the province of Alberta, has of course now drawn another red herring across the path. He can read the news reports as well as I can, and from what I have read the premier of the province indicated that he felt there was some conflict between the private interests of the treasurer and his responsibility as a cabinet minister. In those circumstances he asked for his resignation, and got it. I would hope that this manifestation of principle would be followed by all governments of Canada.
I hope the whole story comes to light.

To get back to the discriminatory action shown on the part of this government in applying these regulations as far as the hospitalization cost sharing program is concerned, let me say this: I wonder what would happen if there were protests in this respect from some of the other provinces

of Canada. Have we reached a point where the only language which this government understands is the language of those who talk tough and are unco-operative? Is this the attitude of a government which makes so much of the spirit of co-operative federalism? Are there to be penalties imposed on those provinces which have chosen to act responsibly and try to administer their affairs and get along with the federal government in a spirit of fair play, reasonableness and cooperation? I should like to remind the members of this government that the price of reasonableness, fair play and co-operation is reasonableness, fair play and co-operation in return.
And justice.

And justice, as my hon. friend says. If the only language this government understands is tough language, then perhaps it is time the government of Alberta began to talk in the kind of terms which will be understood.
We have been trying to secure the fair play about which I spoke. When the new dominion-provincial fiscal arrangements are again before this house, as they will be we hope in a few days, I shall have a great deal more to say about these things because there are at least five different areas in which the province of Alberta in particular because of discriminatory formulae is losing a large percentage of its fair share of the federal moneys redistributed to the provinces. This applies to other provinces, as well. So I think it is time for the government to do what it claims to be doing, that is to see that all the provinces and all the people in Canada are treated alike. Ministers responsible for these matters-and this suggestion has been made several times in the house as being the course actually followed-should not decide how much money they wish to grant to each province and then cook up a formula to provide that predetermined figure. I do not think that is justice. If that is what is done, then of course, it will be the squeaky wheel that gets the grease, and I do not think that is a satisfactory or reasonable way of administering our public affairs.

Mr. Chairman, I would be remiss if I did not say a few words at this stage. If I do so, it is not to delay the committee in any way; I merely wish to make some general remarks about agriculture in Quebec and speak of the slump which affects farmers in that province.

Mr. Chairman, agriculture is truly in a state of depression in Quebec. What is the responsibility of the government under the circumstances? Should it face up to its responsibilities or let agriculture go down like a drifting ship?
For four generations, our farmers have been working for the development, the settling and the expansion of farm land in Quebec; their victory has been achieved at the price of hard work and sacrifices because the means at their disposal were spare indeed.
Today, we have a fertile soil and several farming groups in each community. We have professional farmers with a clear vocation.
As the country and agriculture developed, the farmers' debts increased. After three or four generations, there are practically no more farmers in the province of Quebec who are not in debt up to their necks.
Due to our economic system, all those sacrifices and all those efforts were made under distressing conditions. But yet, that work was done in order to provide a brighter future for generations to come by making available to them the fruits of such labour.
But, Mr. Chairman, our predecessors never worked at such a development for the benefit of only a few individuals who took over the fruits intended for future generations. If there is someone responsible-
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I could draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that the estimates of the Department of Agriculture have been passed and a decision taken on them.

Mr. Chairman, I realize that the agricultural estimates have been passed, but several items among them must be discussed on the occasion of the introduction of interim supply. Indeed, some agricultural items affect this interim supply. I think we can deal with agriculture generally.
The responsibility for that must rest on the old line parties. It is stupid and deceiving to see our national heritage, the very basis of our Canadian economy in the hands of financial interests. The very life of the nation is in the hands of a few unscrupulous people.
For people in debt, the government has no alternative solution than to guarantee the whole economy so that people in debt, those who have been dispossessed can be held in chains and never be free again.
On account of those who are in debt, centralization and collectivism in farming as 20220-389
Interim Supply
well as in all other economic fields are advocated. To protect and respect the financial situation and requirements of a few individuals, some people are ready to sacrifice the work and heritage of generations which have done everything for us and future generations will have nothing to reap, because it will have been necessary to satisfy a few ambitious individuals. Such is the state of mind of the saviours of the people.
Every Canadian citizen including the farmer must abide by an accounting system which robs and discourages the farmer in the first place and has the same effects on the remainder of the community. Those who are responsible will soon have to render an account and their responsibility is constantly increasing.
Therefore, as a result of those startling facts, we must assume our responsibilities. First, as far as farming is concerned, what is to be done? I will say to the government that it is not only with farm loans that it will save agriculture. Agriculture and the other classes of our society will be saved by making them prosperous and by bringing the proper solutions to the true causes of the disorder.
Family farms must be safeguarded. The various governments must take the necessary steps to protect and encourage agriculture.
First of all, solutions different from the ones which were applied in the past must be found. The steps required to help agriculture out of its present stagnation must be taken.
In this regard, I take the liberty of pointing out that everything has been done when our national defence was concerned or when other countries at war needed some assistance. All our economy was set in action. We found the means to give jobs to all the technicians, the engineers and the labourers of the country and to take advantage of all our resources. Money was no object; there was no problem to find the funds required.
When time came to go on with international destruction and slaughter, everything was done and it was done in the name of Christendom and freedom. Members of the government should know that it is also in the name of Christendom and civilization that we must feed and prevent from starving countries that are unable to feed their people. Starvation causes more destruction in various countries than the most devastating of wars.
Consequently, in the name of justice, in the name of civilization, in the name of human beings, let us revive our agriculture, let us

Interim Supply
take the same means as those we used to wage war, let us provide the required equipment and let us put our technicians to work.
It is up to the government to understand and to make available to farmers every mechanical and technical equipment they need.
I will get the following answer: "But the farmers will not be able to repay this money". To get your money back, send the bills to the same place where you sent those for the weapons you threw on Hitler and Mussolini from 1939 to 1945.
You have armoured cars that will never be used, several of which have cost as much as $300,000 each. You spend huge sums of money on aircraft, on war material of no use whatsoever.
At least, if you manufactured farm implements and gave them to farmers, they would serve some logical and practical purpose and to carry out worth-while projects.
For the price of a tank, it would be possible to manufacture several tractors for the farmers; that would greatly help the farm people and would also give work to the people who would manufacture them.
If agriculture is the cornerstone of our society and the mainstay of our economy, why do everything in a niggardly way? Let us do what needs to be done. If agriculture is prosperous, the rest of society will be prosperous also, because it must be recognized that the farmer, in addition to being a producer, is also the most important consumer.
Let us put an end to temporary, piecemeal and inadequate measures, let us get to the heart of the problem, let us help the farm people so that they will no longer depend on the kindness of the other classes of society. We must start at the beginning through an educational program, but we must also realize that this problem can be solved if our farmers can sell their production at a profit, never at a loss as is the case now.
The government should buy any production surplus, supervise storage and find markets through price stabilization, while leaving a reasonable profit, the main problem being one of distribution.
I think that economists or scientists will never be able to teach farmers how to produce pork or beef. The only way is to set a profitable price and establish price stability; in this way, we will have an abundant production.
The government's duty is to supply farmers with the fertilizers they need, the required technique by our farm experts, to give them good equipment, as far as cheap
[Mr. Latulippe.l
machines are concerned; then agriculture will know further developments. Steps should also be taken to make them enjoy the benefits of crop insurance, insurance in case of loss of their cattle, and the guarantee at least of partial repayment. The fear of risk explains to a certain point why some Quebec farms were not and are not entirely developed.
The Canadian Press, itself controlled by press agencies, takes whole pages to analyse false problems and report the actions of royal commissions which have no other purpose but to quiet public opinion, because those who appointed them do not feel strong enough to bring final solutions to situations which are unbelievable nowadays.
The first concern of governments should be the prosperity of agriculture, which might be assured of efficient means like loans without interest, free machines and fertilizers-if necessary-stable markets, equipment at government expense for farm improvement.
Low priced feed grain, government subsidized means of transportation, as the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) announced the other day, government paid drainage, retimbering, water conservation through storage, those give an idea of the problems and the solutions which have to be brought about if we want to make agriculture a paying proposition.
ARDA program will undoubtedly bring about many solutions, but it will not settle all the problems. The officials in charge of the administration of ARDA will have to assess the primary problems in agriculture; they will also have to take into consideration the main advice which will be given them if they want agriculture to be profitable in the province of Quebec and throughout Canada.
Those are, Mr. Chairman, the few remarks I wanted to make.

I maintain that this would be a good thing, in that because of the natural layout of the harbour it would not be very difficult or costly to do so. New construction is now underway to take care of low draft vessels and this could be extended. The deep water is right there and all that would be required would be a vessel bed to carry the ships at low tide.
The argument I get from the department is that there is already a facility for such ships on that shore, but I would hasten to point out that this facility already serves two industries. It serves an industry which is mining barium and another industry which is producing gypsum. The area around the harbour where the wharf is located is very hilly and it is extremely difficult to stockpile wood there so that it can be loaded on ships readily. Even if this could be done, because of the nature of the harbour and the high tides in the area which run twice a day a ship can only move on the crest of the tide. Having in mind the time it takes to load a ship with wood, this would paralyse the port for use by the other two industries. It just will not work out that wood can be loaded at that port. This is one of the main arguments why the government should consider the provision of facilities for ocean-going vessels at Noel.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

In addition to the arguments that the hon. member has just made with regard to the busy nature of the wharf facilities, would he not agree that the need for such facilities at Noel has increased greatly in the past year or so because of the new possibility of greater shipments from that area, if such facilities were provided?

Yes. The need has existed for some years and I would agree that it may be increasing. However there is another angle to this matter. There is a desire to process our natural products there as much as we can before they are exported, and I understand that a study of this matter is under way. Perhaps our pulp and paper producing industries can be expanded and this may take up the slack. But I still say that the federal government has saved enough money on maintenance of wharves because of the wharves which

have been abandoned in that area to spend a few thousand dollars to extend these facilities. I think it would be a move in the right direction, and I am all in favour of anything which is in line with economy. I am not in favour of spending money on something which will not be of economic benefit.
If I may go further, there are other things which could assist this area and are probably related to the forest industry. As I said before, the people of the area rely almost entirely upon the cutting, loading and moving of wood. The government of Nova Scotia in the last few years has been faced with the very heavy burden of constructing roads in that area because now wood is moved by truck much more than it was before. It was necessary to do this because the wharves had been allowed to deteriorate, and there is only the odd wharf available here and there. The area is cut off by a natural barrier known as the Shubenacadie river. To get across the river from the area trucks must travel upstream a distance of about 20 miles and then travel roughly the same distance down the other side to get to the centre of Nova Scotia.
ARDA has been mentioned this afternoon, and I should like to say that there is a strong committee working on the matter of a survey of the river to see if a crossing cannot be established near its mouth. This would make it possible for people to have easy access to the area. It would develop the rural area of East Hants and be of great benefit to the people on both sides of the river. As a matter of fact, even western Nova Scotia would benefit. The committee has been working diligently on a survey of this matter. They have received some voluntary support from the municipal councils and the boards of trade in the surrounding area and also from the province. There is some suggestion that ARDA might participate. I cannot think of a more useful place for ARDA to participate than in the cost of this survey. It is not right to ask the municipalities to underwrite projects of this kind because they are burdened to the hilt now with their own problems involving the cost of education and so on. I would be very pleased if the minister would take note of this to ascertain if the project could not come under ARDA because the cost would only be a few thousand dollars and it would mean a lot to the municipalities in that area.
There is another thing to which I would like to refer, and that is that those in the area who have been displaced in the forest industry have found employment at a radar station known as Beaverbank. Within the

last few months the Department of National Defence has indicated this station will be completely abandoned by September 1. This facility is in excellent shape and should be very useful. I gather the impression from the people down there that they would like the Department of National Defence to use the housing and other facilities there. It is located on a paved highway within 20 miles of Halifax. There are 120 housing units which have all the facilities. There are churches, schools and a recreation centre including a swimming pool. I gained the impression that even the service people think this is a wonderful set-up and would like to take it over. Within the last few days I read in the newspapers that the Associate Minister of National Defence is now going to take a second look at it. I hope he will take a darned good look at it and will be able to bring about something in that area which will be of benefit, not only to the area but the services as well.
I think that in this day and age these facilities are located close to a city and deserve consideration. It is only a 15 or 20 mile drive into the city, and so far as the isolation of the families is concerned, I do not think that is a question because nearly everyone has a family car today. I know there are servicemen with families who live at least 75 miles from their base, and they do not seem to suffer.
In closing, sir, I should like to say that another big problem in Nova Scotia is transportation. Our cost of living in that area is high because a lot of the things we buy have to come from far away. I want to say a word of appreciation to the Atlantic development board for providing $3 million of assistance to our trunk highways. The highway between Halifax and Truro needs to be developed. Traffic is extremely heavy and it needs to be widened. Even if that were done, it would still be more or less out of date. It costs a lot of money to build highways through that type of country. I hope the federal government will continue in an ever growing way to take an interest in the province of Nova Scotia, because the government of that province has worked very hard and done a great deal to bring industries to the province. If the federal government will cease pulling things out of the province and consider putting things into the province, we may keep our people employed and we will be ever grateful.

Mr. Chairman, my interest in the forest goes back to my boyhood days when

my grandfather told me many stories of his exploits as one of the first settlers in our area. The whole district was heavily wooded at that time with great stands of hard maple, ash and other hardwoods, as well as white pine, hemlock, and tamarack and balsam in the swamps.
Forests in those days were an encumbrance, and thousands of acres of excellent timber were cut down and burned so that land could be quickly cleared and made ready for the production of food. Only the very choicest logs were saleable and my grandfather said he sold the choicest white pine for $8 a thousand delivered at the mill in Owen Sound. However, as the area became settled, lumbering emerged as the main industry. Mills were set up throughout the whole district and the exploitation of our great stands of timber was under way.
Conservation was a word never heard, and regardless of whether or not the land was suitable for cultivation, the forest was cleaned off, actually leaving completely devastated areas that were suitable only for timber production. Of course during this timber boom many woodworking plants, by way of secondary industry, were established and were prosperous. However as time progressed and timber limits began to peter out, many of these furniture factories were unable to continue profitably and were forced out of business. The big lumber mills came to the same fate, as the timber being rafted in from the north shore of Georgian bay to support their operations was finished. We do have enough second growth hardwood available, which of course may be supplemented with some imported lumber, to keep several thriving industries in my area under production.
In the city of Owen Sound, R.C.A. Victor has an up to date plant producing television cabinets, and Keenan Woodenware produces a variety of products. In the town of Meaford the Knight families have several factories producing wood products and they have built up an envious reputation as producers of hardwood flooring. Bovell Bros, in Meaford uses a variety of wood in its operations. So, the forest still plays an important part in the economy of the Georgian bay district.
In the summer months thousands of tourists are attracted to our area, mainly because of our beautiful beaches, but we do have some quite extensive well wooded provincial parks with excellent accommodation. While on the subject of parks, I would bring to the attention of the minister the great undeveloped potential for a national park in the Georgian bay country. Perhaps I should direct this to

Interim Supply
the attention of the minister of northern affairs. However what I am about to propose would involve the minister responsible for ARDA.
We have a great ridge running through Grey county that involves some 40,000 acres and which, in my humble opinion, should be completely reforested. This area contains a high percentage of marginal land, and if reforested would serve a more useful purpose. The area reaches an altitude of 1,735 feet above sea level, the highest point in the province of Ontario. This ridge is the watershed for the Humber, the Grand and the Credit rivers running to the south, the Saugeen to the west, and all the rivers and streams flowing north into Georgian bay. If this area were reforested, it would impede the fast spring run-off of all these rivers and eventually restore them to their normal flow. This program and many other similar projects on other watersheds would aid considerably in bringing our great lakes back to normal levels. We must provide more water storage, and forests are a source of assistance. At the present time more water in our great lakes waterway is a dire necessity.
I just noticed in the Globe and Mail yesterday that the loss to shipping and industry is tremendous, and the loss to the iron ore industry alone has been estimated at $13 million. We were made aware of the great loss to other shipping earlier in the debate in this house.
This area is in proximity to the highly populated centres and will, in my opinion, some day be developed as the need for water and recreation become critical. Therefore, I propose that a survey be made so that some of the preliminaries might get under way in connection with reforestation. I should say also that the raising of the levels of the rivers, such as the Sydenham, the Beaver and the Bighead which flow into Georgian bay, would be a shot in the arm for our sport and commercial fishermen. Rainbow trout, which in recent years are becoming more abundant, use these rivers for spawning, and more water means more protection for the fish; more fish mean more tourists.
It has been announced by the Ontario department of lands and forests that they will be stocking Georgian bay and lake Superior with sockeye salmon, and these fish will also use the rivers for spawning. I might be allowed to say, in passing, that I take great satisfaction from the proposed plan for the sockeye, as I made this suggestion on the floor of the house and in the fisheries com-

mittee about six years ago, and have continued to press for action on the matter ever since.
Our forests also make an indirect contribution to the tourist industry by way of giving covering protection and food to our thousands of moose and deer, which provide many tourist dollars as well as providing big game hunting for our own people. This is now a noteworthy industry.
In doing some research on the forestry industry and how it applies to our nation, I was amazed at some of the figures I came across. The pulp and paper industry generates directly or indirectly $1 in eight of the incomes of all Canadians. Three hundred thousand persons are employed in the woods and mills; many other thousands gain work and wages in meeting the needs of this group and of the industry itself, for pulp and paper is the biggest buyer of goods and services of all Canada's manufacturing industries. Ninety pulp and paper companies own 130 mills in eight of the 10 provinces; only in Prince Edward Island and Saskatchewan is pulp and paper not the leading or among the leading industries.
Pulp, newsprint, fine papers, paperboard, building materials, plastics, cellophane, rayon and other textile fabrics, and literally hundreds of commodities classed as essentials have their start in Canada's pulp and paper establishments. Without this industry Canada would not rank today as an important world trader, living standards would be lower, annual labour income and gross national product could not have reached their unprecedented highs. Every hour of the day and night the pulp and paper industry turns out more than 1,000 tons of products valued at $140,000, or $1.3 billion a year. The value of its annual production equals that of wheat and all other grains combined, or of the country's total mineral output. Pulp and paper exports amount to some $981 million dollars annually, approximately a quarter of all Canada's exports, and a third of the nation's exports to the United States.
More than half of the output of the industry is in the form of newsprint, and half of the newspaper pages in the world are printed on Canadian newsprint. The great increase in newspaper circulations throughout the world would not have been possible without Canada's newsprint production. In 1955 Canada consumed about 7 per cent of her newsprint production, 11 per cent went to countries overseas, and 82 per cent was sold in the United States. Newsprint is Canada's leading export.

Nine tenths of Canada's existing forests stand on publicly owned crown lands. Most of the wood used by the pulp and paper industry is cut from crown lands, with payment made to provincial governments for the lease, and for the amount of wood cut. The federal government collects more tax revenue from pulp and paper than from any other industry, and payments to all governments run to some $200 million a year.
Converting our trees into pulp and paper is the most economic use to which most of our forest resources may be put. A tree consumed by the pulp machines leaves virtually no waste. Indeed the industry uses for the most part trees of a size which could never make anything but scrap lumber. The pulp and paper industry accounts for about a fifth of the wood consumed in Canada each year. Fire, insects and disease destroy almost as much, while a similar amount is used annually for fuel, and one and a half times as much is cut for lumber. The industry creates far more new wealth annually than all other forest industries combined.
The paperboard and building board output of the industry is second to newsprint production, and most of these products are consumed in Canada. For shipping containers, paperboard has largely displaced wooden boxes, while for the construction industry there are hardboards and many types of building board. In the manufacture of paperboard and building board the pulp and paper industry is actually conserving the forests, since an equivalent output of material from the sawmills would require the use of many more trees.
Canada's forests cover 1.4 million square miles and the country's forest resources are exceeded in total only by the tropical forests of Brazil and the forests of Russia. Of Canada's total forest area 826,000 square miles are classified as productive, and of this 249,000 square miles are at present economically inaccessible. Demand for raw materials is constantly extending pulpwood operations. Several companies are cutting beyond the height of land on watersheds draining into Hudson's bay, hauling the logs by truck road to the headwaters of streams that flow south to the mills, and through improvements in silviculture and by reduction of losses from fire, insects and disease, more and more wood will be obtained from the forests now occupied.
The fine paper industry, entirely separate from newsprint and pulp production, employs about 27,000 Canadians and has an annual
Interim Supply
output of about $80 million. Its range of products includes book, writing, ledger, currency, blotting and magazine papers; it also includes the paper that goes into drinking cups, milk containers, wallpaper, wedding invitations, cigarette paper and the finest rag paper selling for as much as $1,500 a ton.
Canada's fine paper industry dates back to 1803, when the first mill was established near Lachute, Quebec. Today 18 mills are in operation, many of them on sites chosen a century ago, and the descendants of many of the early papermakers continue in the trade. In Canada, because of the relatively small national population and because the industry's output covers about 500 different products, fine paper is not made on a mass production basis. Also the fine paper industry, unlike the newsprint industry, is faced with tariff barriers that sharply limit exports to foreign markets. Despite these substantial handicaps the fine paper industry provides Canadians with a range of products at prices comparable to those which are obtained in the United States or Great Britain, the two chief fine paper producers of the world.
I think the house will agree that this is a magnificent industry and that every effort should be made to pass it on to posterity a little better than we found it. It does seem, however, that we have a minister in this government who is somewhat careless in respect to the orders he issues when it comes to preserving our forests. The Minister of Transport issued an order a few days ago grounding all 34 Beaver aircraft used by the Ontario department of lands and forests for firefighting. At the time 60 fires were raging in our forests and planes were in urgent need, so much so that two planes came from across the border to help, and they were Beaver aircraft. I would caution the minister to consider the consequences before issuing such orders. He might well have jeopardized the lives of many people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Since the hour is getting rather late I shall be as brief as I can, but I would like to say a few words in regard to the forests in the Atlantic region. The forestry resources of the maritime provinces are one of the most important assets in our area, and it was a significant step taken by the former Conservative administration to establish the Department of Forestry. It was also welcome news to learn at that time that Hon. Hugh John Flemming had consented to assume

Interim Supply
the duties related to the formation of this department. I feel certain that the present minister owes him a great debt of gratitude for the outstanding job he did in establishing the department in the efficient and effective manner that is so evident today.
Soon after the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton assumed the duties associated with his position as minister of forestry, an article appeared in the Atlantic Advocate in which he presented some of his views as to the value of forestry in the Atlantic region. Among other interesting things which he said, and there was a lot of good material in it, he said this:
The Atlantic provinces are fortunate in having 80 million acres of forest. Practically all of it is accessible. About three quarters of the timber is softwood and suitable for the manufacture of pulp and paper.
This asset is of special importance to the Atlantic provinces in view of their ideal location as a base for export to world markets.
Did the hon. member for Kootenay East have something to say?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: There is not as much soft wood as there are soft heads on that side of the house.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
On the question of soft heads, I am sure the hon. member is an authority. However he will have an opportunity to make his own speech, and for the moment I would ask you, Mr. Chairman, to tell him to remain seated on what little brains he has.
The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton continued:
This asset is of special importance to the Atlantic provinces in view of their ideal location as a base for export to world markets. No tariff of importance operates against pulp or paper in the export markets; and economists have forecast that the world demand for these products will double in the next 25 years or less.
Further down in the article, the hon. gentleman had this to say:
With an assured supply of raw materials and the opportunity for continued expansion it is not surprising that the forest industries in the Atlantic provinces play an important role in the regional economy.

speechtext: He is reading somebody else's speech.
They do not care about Nova Scotia.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Undoubtedly the hon. member for Kootenay East has a very loud voice, but I doubt whether he has a strong voice in the present government, even though he is a parliamen-

tary secretary. I hope, Mr. Chairman, you will ask him to close the wide vacant space in his face until I have finished these remarks. My time is very limited so I hope he will allow me to continue, and then say his own little piece when he has an opportunity.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Finish reading your speech.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Extensive forestry resources are to be found in the provinces of New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Nova Scotia and, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, in both New Brunswick and Nova Scotia these resources are easily accessible, and therefore have much greater potential from the development point of view.
At the same time, one of the important aspects associated with forestry is the conservation measures that must be adopted if we are to be able to have the assurance that depletion and wholesale exploitation will not be the end result, with a most necessary and desirable industry disappearing from our area. Better forestry management practices must come and these can only be brought about through educating the population in the provinces in good forestry practices, and through legislation which places restrictions on the manner in which the products from the forests are utilized.
I was interested to note the comments in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald yesterday, July 28, by Nova Scotia's minister of lands and forests, Hon. E. D. Haliburton, who is reported as saying: "The Nova Scotia government is concerned about the quality of forest management on the province's crown lands." He had a good deal more to say, but I have no time to place it all on record. However, I have no doubt it would be of interest to members of this committee and I would refer them to the article in question.
We have the good fortune on Cape Breton island to have seen established in recent years the Nova Scotia Pulp Company which has been utilizing the products of our forests in Nova Scotia, especially from the island of Cape Breton. At the same time we have seen an increasing emphasis on the exporting of lumber to markets overseas. This has resulted in added employment for the people of my area. We have also seen the development of a forestry program by the government of Nova Scotia, in co-operation with the Department of Forestry in Ottawa, initiated during the period when the Conservative party held office, to have the double-barrelled effect of utilizing our forests to the greatest possible

degree and providing employment to displaced miners thrown out of work by the actions of the Dominion Coal Company. This program has proven to be highly successful, to the degree that this government has adopted the program established by the former Conservative administration. However, substantial delays in reaching agreement with the province of Nova Scotia have been evident since this government assumed office. I would like to hear an explanation from the Minister of Forestry as to why these delays have occurred, in view of statements by Premier Stanfield of Nova Scotia that his government is ready and willing to proceed at any time on the basis of the agreement originally reached by the former administration and his government. Certainly hardships were created because of the dilatory attitude of this government in arriving at an agreement with the government of Nova Scotia.
The people of my area and the people of Cape Breton generally are now facing further serious problems as the result of the intended action of a coal operator to curtail coal mining operations on Cape Breton island. The end result can only be more unemployment, hardship and poverty unless immediate action is taken by this government to initiate programs which will provide employment for those thrown out of work. Certainly one of the programs that would assist in this regard would be increased emphasis on the forestry program already in effect. In this regard, I might say that officials of the united mine workers of America will be meeting with Premier Stanfield tomorrow, and among the matters to be discussed is the forest stand improvement program for displaced or unemployed miners. Associated with this forest stand improvement, in my opinion steps should be taken by the present minister to establish a forestry research station on Cape

Breton island. This research station would be designed to increase forest research work throughout the Atlantic provinces. Not only would this station involve itself with the conservation of all of our forest resources but it would also endeavour to increase production and develop new products. It would also endeavour to carry out an educational program in our public schools which would make our young people more aware of the potential of this primary product and provide them with a better appreciation for the utilization of it. It should also endeavour to exert influence on the private owners, both large and small, of our forest lands so that they might better appreciate the importance of conservation and the revitalization of our forest lands.
In conclusion, may I extend to the Minister of Forestry a very cordial invitation to visit Cape Breton island as soon as he can, and see for himself what has been accomplished through the forest stand program. As a result of what he sees he will possibly be more encouraged to establish the forest research station which I have suggested. I thank the rest of the committee for the kindness they have shown in listening to me and, of course, I thank the hon. member for Kootenay East.
Progress reported.
